title: Cyber resilience: SOC foundations
description: Work a SOC queue: read Windows, process and network logs, search and aggregate them like a SIEM, map activity to MITRE ATT&CK, triage alerts, write Sigma detections, detect password spraying and beaconing, and order the first hour of an incident. Defensive only; all data is synthetic.

sources.title: MITRE ATT&CK
sources.licence: ATT&CK terms of use (free, with attribution)

sources.title: Sigma specification and pySigma
sources.used_for: rule format and conversion to SQLite

sources.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
Microsoft: Windows security auditing events 4624 and 4625
sources.used_for: event ids, logon types, status codes

concepts.title: Log sources and what each records
concepts.can_do: Name the log source that answers a given question: authentication, process creation, DNS, network connections.

concepts.title: Windows logon events
concepts.can_do: Read 4624 and 4625 events: logon type, status code, source address.

concepts.title: Process creation events
concepts.can_do: Read Image, CommandLine and ParentImage, and say why a parent-child pair or a command line is suspicious.

concepts.title: Network connection and DNS logs
concepts.can_do: Read a connection record (who, where, port, bytes, duration) and say what it can and cannot tell you.

concepts.title: Searching and filtering normalised logs
concepts.can_do: Filter a log table by field values and patterns to answer a who, what or when question.

concepts.title: Aggregating events
concepts.can_do: Count, count distinct and group events to find the outlier among many sources.

concepts.title: Mapping activity to MITRE ATT&CK
concepts.can_do: Name the ATT&CK tactic and technique for an observed behaviour.

concepts.title: Alert triage
concepts.can_do: Classify an alert as true positive, benign true positive or false positive, set severity and choose the next step.

concepts.title: Writing Sigma rules
concepts.can_do: Write a Sigma rule with the right logsource and a detection that catches the behaviour without flagging known-good activity.

concepts.title: Detecting password spraying
concepts.can_do: Write a detection that flags a source failing against many accounts, and not a single account failing many times.

concepts.title: Detecting beaconing in network data
concepts.can_do: Find a host making small, regular connections to one external address, and rule out approved regular traffic.

concepts.title: The first hour of an incident
concepts.can_do: Order containment, evidence preservation, eradication and recovery, and avoid steps that destroy evidence.

items.prompt: A workstation looked up a suspicious domain name before connecting anywhere. Which log source shows the lookup itself?
hints: Think about which system is asked to turn a name into an address.
The lookup happens before any connection, so connection logs come too late.
It is the log of the name-resolution service.
items.explanation: DNS logs record the query. Firewall and connection logs only show the connection that may follow.

items.prompt: You need to know which program on a laptop opened a suspicious outbound connection. Which pair of sources answers that best?
options: Process creation with command line, and endpoint network events (such as Sysmon event 3)
hints: Network devices see addresses, not programs.
You need a source on the endpoint itself.
One source names the process; the other ties a process to a connection.
items.explanation: Only endpoint telemetry can tie a connection to a process. Network-side logs see the laptop's address, not the program.

items.prompt: Where is an account's logon to a domain-joined file server recorded?
options: The Windows Security log on the server and the domain controller (events 4624 and 4625)
hints: Which system decides whether the logon succeeds?
Windows records it in a specific event log.
Look for the option with event ids.
items.explanation: Windows writes 4624 (success) and 4625 (failure) to the Security log.

items.prompt: What does Windows event 4625 record?
hints: Its partner event, 4624, records a success.
This one records the opposite outcome.
items.explanation: 4625 is 'An account failed to log on'. 4624 is a successful logon.

items.prompt: A 4624 event shows LogonType 3. What kind of logon was it?
options: Network, such as opening a file share
hints: Type 2 is at the keyboard and type 10 is Remote Desktop.
Type 3 happens without anyone sitting at the machine.
Accessing a share over SMB produces it.
items.explanation: LogonType 3 is a network logon. 2 is interactive, 10 is RemoteInteractive (RDP), 5 is a service.

items.prompt: A 4625 event has Status 0xC000006A. What happened?
options: The account exists but the password was wrong
The user name does not exist
hints: Unknown user names produce 0xC0000064.
This code means the account was found.
Something about the secret was wrong.
items.explanation: 0xC000006A is a bad password for an existing account. 0xC0000064 is an unknown user; 0xC0000234 is a locked account.

items.prompt: In a process creation event, which field most often reveals malicious intent?
hints: Legitimate programs such as PowerShell are abused all the time.
So the program's name alone says little.
What matters is what the program was told to do.
items.explanation: Attackers reuse trusted programs, so the command line, and the parent process, carry most of the signal.

items.prompt: PowerShell starts with `-nop -w hidden -enc <long base64 string>`, and its parent is WINWORD.EXE. Why is this suspicious?
options: A document launched a hidden window with an obfuscated command, a common dropper pattern
Base64 means the traffic is encrypted
hints: Look at the parent first: should a word processor start a shell?
Then look at the flags: what do -w hidden and -enc do?
Hidden plus encoded plus an Office parent is the pattern.
items.explanation: Office documents should not spawn shells; a hidden window and an encoded command hide what runs. PowerShell itself is a normal admin tool.

items.prompt: In the process table, an Office application started PowerShell on one workstation. Which host (Computer) was it? Answer with the host name.
hints: Office applications live under ...\Office16\.
Filter on ParentImage, not Image.
Try: SELECT Computer, Image, ParentImage FROM process WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%WINWORD.EXE'
items.reference: SELECT Computer FROM process WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%WINWORD.EXE' AND Image LIKE '%powershell.exe'
items.explanation: Filtering on the parent process finds the child that a document launched.

items.prompt: What does a Zeek conn.log record tell you?
options: The content of the web page
Who connected to whom, on which port, for how long, with how many bytes
The user name of the person browsing
hints: Zeek watches traffic on the wire.
Encrypted payloads are not readable there.
It records the metadata of each connection.
items.explanation: Connection logs are metadata: endpoints, port, protocol, duration and bytes. No users, no processes, no decrypted content.

items.prompt: Which pattern is the strongest network sign of command-and-control beaconing?
options: Connections at near-constant intervals, with similar small sizes, to one external address
Many DNS queries to a CDN
hints: Malware checks in with its server on a timer.
Check-ins are small: 'any jobs for me?'
Regular and small, to one place.
items.explanation: Beacons are periodic, small and repetitive. Port 443 alone says nothing; most traffic uses it.

items.prompt: One source address in 10.0.9.0/24 appears in the auth table. Which address is it?
hints: Filter IpAddress with a pattern.
LIKE '10.0.9.%' matches the range.
SELECT DISTINCT IpAddress FROM auth WHERE IpAddress LIKE '10.0.9.%'
items.reference: SELECT DISTINCT IpAddress FROM auth WHERE IpAddress LIKE '10.0.9.%'
items.explanation: A pattern filter on a normalised field narrows millions of events to one source.

items.prompt: Which account logged on successfully (EventID 4624) from the 10.0.9.x address? Answer with the user name.
hints: First find the 10.0.9.x address.
Then keep only successful logons from it.
WHERE IpAddress LIKE '10.0.9.%' AND EventID = 4624
items.reference: SELECT TargetUserName FROM auth WHERE IpAddress LIKE '10.0.9.%' AND EventID = 4624
items.explanation: A success after a run of failures from the same source is the moment a spray becomes an incident.

items.prompt: How many distinct accounts did the 10.0.9.x source try to log on as (failures and successes together)? Answer with a number.
hints: Count accounts, not events.
COUNT(DISTINCT TargetUserName).
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT TargetUserName) FROM auth WHERE IpAddress LIKE '10.0.9.%'
items.reference: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT TargetUserName) FROM auth WHERE IpAddress LIKE '10.0.9.%'
items.explanation: Distinct targets per source is the signal of a spray; raw event counts are not.

items.prompt: One external destination in the conn table receives far more connections than any other. Which destination IP is it?
hints: Group by destination.
Order by the count, largest first.
SELECT dst_ip, COUNT(*) AS n FROM conn GROUP BY dst_ip ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 5
items.reference: SELECT dst_ip FROM conn GROUP BY dst_ip ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1
items.explanation: Stacking (grouping and sorting counts) surfaces the outlier among many sources.

items.prompt: Which MITRE ATT&CK technique is password spraying?
options: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
hints: Spraying is a way of guessing credentials.
It is a sub-technique of guessing many passwords.
Look under Brute Force.
items.explanation: Password spraying is sub-technique .003 of Brute Force (T1110), under the Credential Access tactic.

items.prompt: Word starts hidden, encoded PowerShell. Which technique describes the PowerShell execution itself?
options: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
hints: Which tactic is 'running code'?
Execution.
The interpreter is named in the technique.
items.explanation: T1059.001 under Execution. The macro document that delivered it is a separate technique (phishing attachment, T1566.001).

items.prompt: An infected host checks in with an attacker's server over HTTPS every minute. Which ATT&CK tactic is that?
hints: The host is asking for instructions, not sending data out in bulk.
Which tactic covers talking to the attacker's infrastructure?
items.explanation: Command and Control (TA0011), technique T1071.001 Web Protocols. Exfiltration is moving data out.

items.prompt: Alert: 12 failed logons (Status 0xC000006A) for svc_backup in one hour, from 10.0.2.40, the backup server's own address. No successes. The account's password was rotated yesterday. How do you classify it?
options: True positive, high: brute force in progress
Benign true positive: real failures from a service still using the old password; fix the service and close
False positive: the rule logic is broken
Ignore it: service accounts are not monitored
hints: The rule fired on events that really happened.
Is there an attacker in the story?
A real but harmless match has its own name.
items.explanation: The detection worked; the activity is real but harmless. That is a benign true positive. A false positive means the rule matched something it should not have.

items.prompt: Alert: 22 different accounts fail to log on from 10.0.9.150 within three minutes, then one account succeeds from the same address. What is it, and what comes first?
options: True positive, high: a spray that succeeded; disable or reset the account that logged on and scope its activity
True positive, low: only failures matter
hints: Many accounts, one source, short time.
Then a success from the same source.
A successful spray means one credential is now known to the attacker.
items.explanation: A spray with a success is a compromised credential. Contain the account first, then scope what it did.

items.prompt: The 'Encoded PowerShell' rule fires on 300 machines at 02:00. The parent is CcmExec.exe, the configuration manager agent, and change records show a scheduled software deployment. What do you do?
options: True positive, critical: isolate all 300 machines
Benign true positive: confirm with the deployment owner, then add a narrow exclusion for that parent and record why
hints: Is there evidence of an attacker, or of a planned change?
Deleting the rule would also hide the real thing.
Tune narrowly, and write down why.
items.explanation: Verify with the owner, then tune with the narrowest exclusion (this parent), documented. Deleting the rule blinds you to real encoded PowerShell.

items.prompt: In a Sigma rule, which section says which logs the rule applies to?
hints: The converter needs to know which table or index to search.
The section's name says where the logs come from.
items.explanation: logsource (category, product, service) picks the logs; detection holds the selections; condition combines them.

items.prompt: Write a Sigma rule (logsource: category process_creation, product windows) that detects PowerShell started with an encoded command. It must catch the malicious event and must not flag the backup script or ordinary PowerShell use. Fields available: Image, CommandLine, ParentImage, User, Computer.
hints: Two conditions: the program is PowerShell, and the command line carries an encoded-command flag.
Use Image|endswith for the program and CommandLine|contains for the flag. PowerShell accepts shortened flags.
Cover ' -enc', ' -e ' and ' -EncodedCommand' (matching is case-insensitive).
items.reference:
title: Encoded PowerShell
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ' -enc'
      - ' -e '
  condition: selection_img and selection_cmd
level: high
items.explanation: Pair the program with the suspicious flag; either alone is too broad. ' -enc' also matches -EncodedCommand.

items.prompt: Write a Sigma rule (category process_creation, product windows) that detects an Office application (Word, Excel or PowerPoint) starting PowerShell. It must not flag PowerShell started from Explorer or by services.
hints: This rule is about the parent-child pair, not the command line.
ParentImage|endswith takes a list of Office executables.
Combine a parent selection and an Image|endswith '\powershell.exe' selection with 'and'.
items.reference:
title: Office spawning PowerShell
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\WINWORD.EXE'
      - '\EXCEL.EXE'
      - '\POWERPNT.EXE'
  child:
    Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
  condition: parent and child
level: high
items.explanation: Parent-child rules catch the delivery step no matter how the command line is disguised.

items.prompt: Why does 'many failed logons from one source' make a poor password-spray detection?
options: A spray tries few passwords per account across many accounts, so the signal is distinct accounts per source; counting failures also flags one service account failing repeatedly
hints: How many times does a spray try each account?
What else produces many failures from one place?
items.explanation: Spraying avoids lockouts by trying each account once or twice. Count distinct target accounts per source in a time window.

items.prompt: Write a SQL query over the auth table whose first column lists every source IP you would alert on for password spraying. The misconfigured service account that fails many times from its own server must not be flagged, and neither must users who mistype once or twice.
hints: Group the failed logons (EventID 4625) by source.
Count distinct accounts per source, not events.
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TargetUserName) >= 10
items.reference: SELECT IpAddress FROM auth WHERE EventID = 4625 GROUP BY IpAddress HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TargetUserName) >= 10
items.explanation: Distinct accounts per source separates a spray from a lockout loop and from typos.

items.prompt: Write a SQL query over the conn table whose first column lists the internal hosts (src_ip) that are beaconing. The update agent that checks in hourly with 198.51.100.200 is approved infrastructure.
hints: Group by source and destination together.
Beacons are many connections with small, similar sizes.
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 AND AVG(bytes_out) < 500
items.reference: SELECT src_ip FROM conn GROUP BY src_ip, dst_ip HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 AND AVG(bytes_out) < 500
items.explanation: Volume plus small, uniform size per source-destination pair finds the beacon; the hourly updater is regular but rare.

items.prompt: Roughly how often does the beaconing host check in? Answer in seconds (within 5 seconds counts).
hints: Find the beaconing pair first.
Look at the gaps between consecutive timestamps.
LAG(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts) with julianday() gives the gap; multiply by 86400 for seconds.
items.reference: SELECT ROUND(AVG(gap)) FROM (SELECT (julianday(ts) - julianday(LAG(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts))) * 86400 AS gap FROM conn WHERE dst_ip LIKE '203.0.113.%')
items.explanation: A stable gap between check-ins, plus a little jitter, is the beacon's period.

items.prompt: Ransom notes are appearing on file server SRV-FILE01 and files are being encrypted now. Put these first steps in order, as a comma-separated list of letters.

steps.text: Isolate the server from the network, keeping it powered on
Preserve volatile evidence: memory and running processes
Find the entry point and the compromised account, and reset it
Restore files from known-good offline backups
Notify the incident lead and start the incident log

hints: What stops the damage spreading?
Restoring before the cause is removed invites re-infection.
Containment, then eradication, then recovery.
items.reference: A, B, E, C, D (E may come anywhere before D)
items.explanation: Contain first, keep evidence, remove the cause, then recover. Restoring early is the most common costly mistake.

items.prompt: While containing an infected server, which action destroys evidence you may need?
options: Blocking the attacker's IP at the firewall
hints: Where do running processes and encryption keys live?
What happens to memory when power is lost?
items.explanation: Memory is lost at power-off, along with running processes and sometimes encryption keys. Isolate instead.

items.prompt: In the NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 incident response life cycle, which phase includes restoring systems from backup?
hints: Restoring is the 'get back to normal' step.
It shares a phase with removing the threat.
items.explanation: Rev. 2 has four phases; recovery sits with containment and eradication. Rev. 3 (2025) maps the same work to the CSF 2.0 Respond and Recover functions.
